CausalChain: Epigenetic dysregulation in tumors -> DNA methylation represses CLDN18.2 expression -> Use DNMT inhibitors to reverse methylation -> Increased transcription and surface expression of CLDN18.2 on tumor cells -> Higher target density for CLDN18.2-directed therapies (monoclonal antibodies/CAR-T cells) -> Enhanced antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity and T-cell mediated tumor lysis -> Improved antitumor immune response and clinical outcomes
Hypothesis: Epigenetic modulation through DNA methyltransferase inhibition can selectively increase CLDN18.2 expression in gastric tumor cells, thereby sensitizing these cells to CLDN18.2-targeted immunotherapies and overcoming microenvironment-driven resistance.
Abstract: This study proposes a novel therapeutic strategy that leverages epigenetic modulation to upregulate CLDN18.2 expression specifically within gastric tumor cells, thereby enhancing their vulnerability to CLDN18.2‐targeted immunotherapies. Epigenetic alterations, such as DNA methylation changes, are known to regulate CLDN18.2 transcription. Inhibition of DNA methyltransferases may remove these repressive marks and potentiate the expression of CLDN18.2 on tumor cells. Increased antigen density in turn could amplify the efficacy of immune-mediated cytotoxicity elicited by monoclonal antibodies, bispecific antibodies, and CAR-T cells. This hypothesis is bolstered by preclinical observations that chemotherapeutic agents, which modify epigenetic landscapes, upregulate CLDN18.2 and synergize with targeted therapies. The proposed approach may overcome challenges posed by tumor microenvironment heterogeneity and immunosuppressive signaling, creating a more robust antitumor immune response.
